✅ According to a report from one of the well-known publishers and bookstores, the best-selling book in Tehran's bookstores over the past few months has been Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Those with greater financial means have bought Jalal Khaleghi-Motlagh's multi-volume critical edition, while those with lower incomes have settled for the single-volume Shahnameh of the Moscow print.

✅ This is happening at a time when book prices have risen sharply, and even 250- or 300-page books sometimes reach around one million tomans; as a result, the era of the physical book is more exposed to decline than ever before. 🔴 Why do even good things sometimes make us feel bad? ✍️ Mostafa Malekian

We usually assume that if good things happen to us, we'll feel good too. But the pleasantness of an event, in itself, doesn't guarantee that we can handle it well.

We live in a world that can be hard on us in two ways: not everything goes the way we want, and we have no certainty about what's coming.

▪️ The world has no obligation to fulfill our desires

There's no reason all the world's events should conform to our preferences and wishes. Some events are pleasant and some unpleasant; even a single event can make one person happy and another miserable.

Rain is a source of joy for a farmer waiting to water his field; but for a launderer who has hung washed clothes out to dry in the sun, it spells trouble.

The rain is the same rain; what differs is its relation to our desires and circumstances. The world has neither sworn to be our enemy nor promised to always go along with what we want.

▪️ Even joys may show up uninvited

The difficulty isn't just that we dislike certain events; it's also that we don't know what will come, or when.

Suppose you love someone dearly, but they show up at your door unannounced. Despite being happy to see them, you might lose your composure and fail to receive them the way you'd like.

Loving a guest is not the same as being ready for their arrival.

The same holds for the good things in life: we may want something, yet not be prepared for its sudden arrival. As a result, our reaction may be ill-considered and create fresh problems.

▪️ The suffering of the event and the suffering of the reaction

Part of life's difficulty comes from events not matching our desires; another part can stem from how we face them.

If we expect life to always unfold according to our wishes and predictions, we'll be constantly caught off guard. And being caught off guard can push us into reactions that only deepen our suffering.

So we must prepare ourselves to live in a world that holds both adversity and uncertainty—so that we can meet what arrives uninvited with greater composure.

We can't control the arrival of every uninvited guest; but we can learn how to face them.

For complex human problems, we shouldn't be looking for technical answers! If a pipe in your house bursts, that's a technical problem; but when your neighbor puts their trash out earlier than they're supposed to, that's no longer merely technical — it belongs to the realm of human problems. In teaching problem-solving, the first thing we draw the learner's attention to is distinguishing the technical problem from the human problem, and when we talk about problem-solving and teaching it, we mean the second category — because technical problems require expertise in their own field. If my phone stops working, I go to a specialist and they fix it. But human problems don't necessarily have predetermined solutions, and technical expertise alone won't help solve them. The solution to these problems has to be discovered, and solving them requires a basic understanding of the humanities and learning the skill of problem-solving. The biggest mistake is usually offering technical solutions for problems with human roots. When my employees' motivation is low and they show up late to work because of it, I can't force them into line with punishment, incentives, and a few new rules; I need to ask why their motivation has dropped, invite them into a conversation, and address the problem at the level of human relationships. Another mistake is assuming that our technical expertise can help us solve human problems — which it absolutely cannot. Yet another mistake is framing problems with human roots in technical terms. In that same example of lateness, if I say the reason is that they wake up late and that a morning phone call will get them to work on time, I've framed a human problem in technical terms! Mistaking technical problems for human ones and vice versa, offering technical solutions for human problems, and expecting clear technical solutions for complex problems — these are among the greatest plagues of our country's decision-making and problem-solving system. In this regard, the Iranian opposition abroad is hardly innocent either! We Iranians don't have strong problem-solving skills, and at the root of this situation you can feel the hegemony of engineers and physicians, the failure of humanities scholars to engage with concrete problems, and the jurists who want to solve human problems through technical legislation. This pattern shows itself when Hezbollahis are waiting for the leadership to solve the problem, the general public is waiting for the government, and some are waiting for Trump! New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools

In the second half of the 1990s, some households, arguing that schools were not religious enough, pulled their children out of school and created a form of home-schooling. The COVID-19 outbreak further entrenched this situation, albeit on a very limited scale. Out of this current, mosque-schools gradually took shape; first established in Qom, they grew rapidly, and today they have branches in 22 provinces and operate under a central headquarters. The number of these schools has doubled over the past 4 years, surpassing 450; with an average of about 30 students per school. After several years of operation, these schools finally obtained operating licenses starting in 1402 as a type of non-governmental school, and they also signed agreements with the government to expand into rural areas. Because these schools use mosque facilities, their tuition is lower, and in addition to more religious instruction, they offer skill-training and income-generation programs; especially income generation through cyberspace and cryptocurrencies.

Alongside this current, a trend of establishing home-schools has also begun in Tehran and is rapidly growing. These are also schools with a student body of between 20 and 40, with very high tuition, often run with supplementary curricula and in more private settings. Many of these home-schools are in practice smaller branches of a private school or affiliated with one. Despite the Ministry of Education's current opposition, these schools do not conflict with the general logic of policymaking in the ministry and face no obstacle to expansion. Home-schools are in the early stages of consolidation, and their activities have so far been reported in some areas of Tehran as well as the metropolises of Tabriz and Isfahan.

The expansion of these micro-schools signals the continuation and intensification of differentiation and the ever-increasing stratification of parts of society into smaller units; a kind of intra-group and intra-class fragmentation. Mosque-schools represent a form of differentiation among more religious families themselves, just as home-schools represent further differentiation among the upper strata of society. These schools should not be conflated with diversity in the educational system, because educational diversity is positive only when it is accompanied by universal access and the possibility of genuine choice for all social groups. Although these schools currently account for a negligible share of the educational system, they are important in terms of institutional analysis.@Omidi_Reza

New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools

In the second half of the 1990s, some households, arguing that schools were not religious enough, pulled their children out of school and created a form of home-schooling. The COVID-19 outbreak further entrenched this arrangement, albeit on a very limited scale. Out of this current, mosque-schools gradually took shape; first established in Qom, they multiplied rapidly and today have branches in 22 provinces, overseen by a central headquarters. Over the past 4 years, the number of these schools has more than doubled to over 450, with an average of roughly 30 students per school. After several years of operation, these schools were finally granted operating licenses starting in 1402 as a type of non-governmental school, and they also signed agreements with the government to expand into rural areas. Because these schools use mosque facilities, their tuition is lower, and beyond more extensive religious instruction, they also offer skills training and income-generation programs—particularly income generation through cyberspace and cryptocurrencies.

Alongside this current, a trend of establishing home-schools has also emerged, starting in Tehran and growing rapidly. These too are schools with a student body of between 20 and 40, charging very high tuition, and are often run with supplementary curricula in more private settings. Many of these home-schools are in practice smaller branches of, or affiliated with, a private school. Despite the Ministry of Education's current opposition, these schools do not conflict with the ministry's overall policy logic and face no obstacle to expansion. Home-schools are in the early stages of becoming established, and their activities have so far been reported in some areas of Tehran as well as the metropolises of Tabriz and Isfahan.

The spread of these micro-schools signals the continuation and intensification of differentiation and the ever-increasing stratification of parts of society into smaller units—a kind of intra-group and intra-class fragmentation. Mosque-schools represent a form of differentiation among more religious families themselves, just as home-schools represent further differentiation among the upper strata of society. These schools should not be conflated with diversity in the educational system, because educational diversity is positive only when it is accompanied by universal access and the possibility of genuine choice for all social groups. Although these schools currently account for a negligible share of the educational system, they are significant in terms of institutional analysis.@Omidi_Reza

Gentlemen in charge! A society squeezed economically by war, sanctions, and siege becomes more sensitive, more on edge, and more vulnerable. The smallest social friction in such an environment carries a far higher cost than under normal conditions. A family grappling with inflation, job insecurity, anxiety over medicine, housing, and their children's future has far less capacity to absorb new tensions. At this point, the quality of social policy is directly linked to the country's ability to navigate the crisis. Every policy must be measured by a simple question: Does this policy, at this moment, strengthen social bonds or further inflame existing fractures? Provocative identity debates, cultural disputes such as hijab, the proposal to lash a female singer, the widespread criminalization of social behavior, measures that pit parts of society against other parts, and the reopening of cases like women's dress code are not merely cultural or legal matters. Under crisis conditions, these policies carry a secondary consequence as well: they divert part of society's political, disciplinary, and psychological energy away from the main problem and activate divisions that — you must accept — Iranian society has moved past and the people deserve respect for, yet under economic pressure these divisions have the potential to turn into social fractures. In this sense, a country in crisis needs something akin to a "social ceasefire" — meaning preventing the creation of conflicts that are not urgent and that can drain the country's limited social capital.

National Wealth Fund

This Oxford Handbook on sovereign wealth funds has gotten a bit dated (2017). Especially in the financial and investment industry, which has seen rapid changes. But its structure, the framework it offers, and the points it makes about the architecture of sovereign wealth funds are truly excellent.

You probably know that one of the most famous funds belongs to Norway, where the government saves and invests oil revenues through a mechanism. They call it an intergenerational perspective. Their government says the state has no right to spend oil money recklessly, because it also belongs to future generations.

They started thirty years ago. Now it's around 2,400 billion dollars. That's roughly half a million dollars per Norwegian.

Interestingly, nearly 70 percent of this money is the returns generated by the oil money itself that have been added to the fund. In one chapter of this book, it examines this fund's policies, which was interesting. One of them is that they never take more than a 10% stake (with voting rights) in any company, so they don't have to get involved in the day-to-day affairs of companies. It should just be an investment and they take their money.

From this perspective, they differ from approaches like Saudi Arabia's (PIF), which uses national money to buy large stakes in companies.

🔶 Mohammad Darvish: Desalinating Oman Sea water is choosing between bad and worse

The government of Masoud Pezeshkian inaugurated the first phase of the project to transfer water from the Oman Sea to the Central Plateau on the 15th of Azar — a plan that Isfahan's industries see as a lifesaver, but some experts warn about its environmental consequences, its energy intensity, and the threat it poses to the Makran coast.

In this context, Mohammad Darvish, an environmental activist, stressed in an interview with Deutsche Welle Persian that "implementing the desalination project for the Oman Sea and transferring water to Isfahan could have far fewer adverse environmental and security consequences than implementing projects to transfer water from the headwaters of the Karun and Dez to Isfahan."

He added: "Unfortunately, the insistence on carrying out projects such as Cheshmeh Langan and Khodangestan and drying up two headwaters of the Dez River, pursuing destructive projects such as the Mandegan Dam and diverting the Marbor River from the headwaters of the Karun, the Khersan 3 Dam and the Beheshtabad project, the plan to transfer water from the Zayandeh Rud to Yazd, and drawing water from the Zayandeh Rud to develop certain orchards have dealt the biggest blow to the resilience of the Dez, Karun, and Zayandeh Rud watersheds and have fueled widespread discontent in the region."

Darvish concludes that "desalinating sea water itself has worrisome environmental consequences, but when choosing between bad and worse, it is preferable."

At the same time, this environmental activist warns that "this water should not be spent on further industrial development and implementing more projects in Isfahan," and adds: "Additional pressure on the provinces of Isfahan, Yazd, and Markazi in the form of polluting and water-intensive industries must be stopped."

Within each of us dwells a sultan and a shepherd. The sultan rules and controls; the inner shepherd guides. The sultan leans toward subjugation, domination, and the management of affairs, while the shepherd leans toward guidance, opening new horizons, and stepping into the unknown.

The sultan is necessary for managing affairs; the shepherd, for creation, bringing forth, and breaking down the walls of human limitation. Sultanhood gravitates toward the individual; shepherdliness, toward the collective.

Yes, both the sultan and the shepherd are needed, but if we are to envision an ultimate destination, that destination is the passage from the inner sultanate to the inner shepherdliness.

Shepherdliness and leadership, then, are not a position. Leadership is a particular way of thinking and being; leadership is a path — in the first instance a personal path that then becomes determinate outwardly and takes on a collective form. The question: shepherd or sultan?

In the process leading to the Islamic Revolution, Iranian society managed to pass beyond sultanate and activate its inner shepherd — and it was this discovered inner shepherd that emerged outwardly, and from its heart, the concept of "Imam" was born. In Iran, leadership emerged because every human being saw themselves as a leader; because leadership emerged as a way of being; because an inner revolution took place in our inner states, and this caused leadership as a collective matter to also appear in Article 43 of the Constitution: "The organization of the country's economic program... such that every individual... has sufficient ability to participate actively in the leadership of the country..."

Once again our inner sultanic relations were activated, and we were degraded from leaders who discovered "leaders" to followers who merely follow. From then on, following, imitation, and the rejection of responsibility became our common behavioral currency. Everywhere: politics, art, culture, economy...

To solve Iran's problems, each of us must first and once again become a leader. We must pass beyond our inner sultanates and activate our inner shepherds; and it is these inner shepherds that, when actualized, make shepherdliness possible outwardly. Let us activate our inner shepherd.

Let us all be leaders.

If we were to describe any figure with a single word, the word that fits Ayatollah Seyyed Mousa Shubeyri Zanjani (who passed away last night) is "mediator."

Despite being considered, in terms of his jurisprudential orientation, among the traditionalist jurists of the seminary, and despite not being devoid of taste or conviction in politics and history—as is evident from his scattered remarks and writings (including in the highly readable book collection "A Sip from the Sea")—he had his own distinct and particular social and political demeanor. In the past two or three decades, he played a role that others were incapable of fulfilling: the role of "mediator" between the system and the religious currents and individuals it had cast out. Shubeyri Zanjani was a "dragoman" for translating the words of two groups who did not understand each other's language. That is why knots that could not be untied through law and conventional political methods were sometimes loosened by a single phone call from him, and challenges that could have spiraled into crises were sometimes defused by a single piece of advice from him. These mediations were, of course, typically behind the scenes and never publicized—and that, too, was part of his way of being.

Because of this role he played, Shubeyri was beloved by all sides. He both associated with the martyred Leader and would recite the funeral prayer for clerics critical of the system, and the door of his home remained open every day to all political and religious currents. Undoubtedly, his humble and tolerant character also contributed to this.

In religious matters as well, although he is classified among the traditional jurists, he took a different approach there too. Unlike them, he did not use his position, standing, and influence to pursue religious identity-driven concerns, and did not seek to pile up a calendar of Shia occasions and to fatten rituals. On the contrary, he was critical of the excessive expansion of rituals.

That said, if the loss of Mr. Shubeyri Zanjani is considered a scholarly loss for the seminaries, it will be a functional and institutional blow for the system and for Iranian society as well—one that could disrupt the relations between the system and certain seminary and religious currents. Although Shubeyri was not considered among the first-tier maraji' in terms of the organizational structure of the marja'iyya, and did not have extensive organizations and numerous offices, and the number of his followers did not extend beyond the circle of certain seminary elites and his fellow townspeople, his loss creates a void in the institution of Shia marja'iyya in Iran that cannot be filled—especially in the current critical conditions, when Iranian society, more than ever, needs those who play the role of mediator in various arenas.

Cooperation with Iran hasn't been insignificant either. But sanctions, banking restrictions, and other considerations have made the scale of cooperation different.

The horizon China has for B&R spans several decades. And naturally, it aligns the decisions, policies, and resources it allocates with this project as much as possible.

In a way, you could call it a super-framework for economic and investment affairs.

It seems to me that friends who these days are looking to analyze the current situation in the Middle East and examine possible future scenarios are paying particularly close attention to Iran, America, and the role of regional players, while giving China a smaller share of attention.

Yet China's decisions in recent years have played an important role in the region – both in places where it intervened contrary to expectations, such as Iran-Saudi relations, and in places where, despite expectations, it did not intervene or intervened only very minimally.

The first thing that usually comes to mind is that China is almost the only buyer of Iran's oil, and from another angle, Iran is a cheap energy supplier and a source of access to mines and underground resources for China.
